title: I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab
outcome: By a 6:5 majority the Court held that Parliament could not amend the Constitution so as to abridge or take away Fundamental Rights. The Seventeenth Amendment was saved by prospective overruling.
ratio: Constitutional amendments are 'law' within the meaning of Article 13(2) and cannot abridge Fundamental Rights.

key_holdings.holding: Fundamental Rights cannot be abridged by constitutional amendment

summary: Golaknath is the immediate precursor to the Basic Structure Doctrine. An 11-judge bench held that Parliament could not use Article 368 to abridge Fundamental Rights. Kesavananda later replaced this absolute bar with the more durable basic-structure limitation.
content_for_rag:
I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab, AIR 1967 SC 1643; (1967) 2 SCR 762, decided on 27 February 1967 by an 11-judge bench, is the leading pre-Kesavananda authority on the amending power. The petitioners challenged land-reform legislation protected by the Constitution (Seventeenth Amendment) Act, 1964, arguing that Parliament could not abridge Fundamental Rights.

By a 6:5 majority, the Court held that a constitutional amendment is 'law' under Article 13(2). Therefore Parliament could not amend the Constitution so as to take away or abridge rights in Part III. Chief Justice Subba Rao also invoked prospective overruling, so that earlier amendments (including the Seventeenth Amendment) were not struck down.

Golaknath created an absolute bar on amending Fundamental Rights. That absolute bar was later replaced in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) 4 SCC 225: Parliament may amend Fundamental Rights, but it cannot damage or destroy the basic structure. Golaknath remains essential to the lineage of the amending-power cases.
